title: Pharmacogenetic Impact of CYP2C19 Variants on Diazepam Treatment Outcomes in Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome.
abstract: Diazepam (DZP) is widely accepted as an effective pharmaceutical intervention for treating Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome (AWS), and its efficacy and metabolic profile are influenced by genetic variations in the CYP2C19 gene. The objective of the present study was to investigate the impact of the CYP2C19*2 and CYP2C19*17 phenotypes on DZP metabolism. Whole blood samples were collected from 114 patients with AWS following a 10-day course of oral DZP therapy. Genotyping was performed using PCR-RFLP. Plasma concentrations of DZP and nordiazepam (NDZP) were determined using HPLC-UV. The CYP2C19*17 TT genotype (1.597 ± 0.589) showed a significantly higher metabolic ratio (MR) compared to CC (1.159 ± 0.423) and CT (1.374 ± 0.368) genotypes (p = 0.015). Withdrawal severity after treatment was significantly lower in TT carriers than in CC and CT genotypes (p = 0.043). Pharmacokinetic and clinical parameters varied across CYP2C19 diplotypes, with ultrarapid (*17/*17) and rapid (*1/*17) metabolisers demonstrating higher MR and lower withdrawal severity compared to extensive metabolisers (*1/*1). The CYP2C19*2 haplotype was associated with higher dose-normalised DZP concentrations, whereas CYP2C19*17 was associated with a higher metabolic ratio. This study is the first to quantify plasma DZP and NDZP levels after 10-day oral administration and link them to CYP2C19*2 and CYP2C19*17 genotypes, haplotypes and diplotypes. The metabolic ratio (NDZP/DZP) emerged as a more integrative indicator of CYP2C19 activity than absolute levels, highlighting the complex genotype-phenotype relationship in DZP metabolism. Notably, the CYP2C19*17 gain-of-function allele significantly was associated with increased metabolic efficiency and improved clinical outcomes in AWS.

title: Adolescent-onset regular cannabis use is associated with altered neural and behavioural responses during anticipation and feedback of monetary reward and loss.
abstract: Regular cannabis use has been associated with alterations in reward-related neural processes, yet findings remain inconsistent and the relationship between neural activity and behavioural performance is not fully understood. The present study aimed to characterise neural and behavioural correlates of reward processing in regular cannabis users (CU) compared with matched non-users (NU) using the Monetary Incentive Delay Task (MIDT). Twenty adolescent-onset regular cannabis users (CU; ≥4 days/week for 2 years, with regular use initiated before age 18) and twenty age- and sex-matched non-users (NU) completed the Monetary Incentive Delay Task during functional MRI. Firstly, we assessed behavioural performance through reaction times, accuracy and monetary earnings to determine whether potential neural alterations were reflected in task performance. Secondly, focusing on reward-related brain regions, we examined group differences in BOLD functional MRI activity during anticipation and outcome phases separately for monetary win and loss conditions. Finally, we explored the association between behavioural performance and neural activation. Our findings provide preliminary evidence that adolescent-onset regular cannabis use is associated with altered engagement of key nodes within the mesocorticolimbic circuit accompanied by impaired behavioural performance. Particularly, compared with NU, CU showed (I) lower striatal activity during anticipation of monetary win and higher ventral striatum and frontal pole activity during anticipation of monetary loss; (II) different VTA BOLD contrast estimates during outcome of successful monetary win and loss avoidance, and lower frontal pole activity during outcome of unsuccessful loss avoidance; (III) lower monetary rewards and a trend towards slower reaction times and reduced accuracy; (IV) disrupted brain-behaviour coupling. Results from this study may help inform future research on the neurobiological mechanisms underlying changes in reward function and the resultant behavioural consequences of adolescent-onset cannabis use.

title: Beyond psychedelic exceptionalism: how people combine meditation with psychoactive substances, and how this relates to well-being.
abstract: Combining meditation with psychoactive substances is often assumed to be a niche practice centred on classic psychedelics. We sought to broaden this narrative in two cross-sectional studies. Study 1 used a broad naturalistic sample (N = 1,391) to examine the prevalence of substance use, meditation, and their simultaneous combination, as well as associations with subjective happiness. Study 2 used a stratified subsample (n = 397) focusing on classic psychedelic and cannabis users, the most common psychedelic-type substances combined with meditation, to assess associations with mental well-being, peace of mind, psychological flexibility, depression, and anxiety. Contrary to prevailing assumptions, alcohol (29%), cannabis (19%), and nicotine (16%) were far more commonly combined with meditation than classic psychedelics (6%). Classic psychedelic use was also embedded within a pattern of pronounced polysubstance use, suggesting that it may reflect a broader substance-use profile rather than an isolated behavioural practice. Regression analyses found no consistent associations between psychedelic or cannabis use, with or without meditation, and any outcome. However, an unexpected pattern emerged for other drugs and alcohol. Other- drug use without meditation was associated with poorer well-being outcomes relative to no other-drug use, whereas other-drug use combined with meditation was not. Alcohol combined with meditation was associated with better well-being outcomes relative to alcohol use without meditation. These findings suggest that combining meditation with substance use is not limited to psychedelics and should be studied within broader patterns of polysubstance use and meditation practice.

title: Prognostic Factors for Neurological Outcome After Surgery for Idiopathic Spinal Cord Herniation: A Systematic Review and Published Individual Patient Data Analysis.
journal: European spine journal : official publication of the European Spine Society, the European Spinal Deformity Society, and the European Section of the Cervical Spine Research Society
abstract: Idiopathic spinal cord herniation (ISCH) is a rare cause of progressive thoracic myelopathy, for which surgical management is widely accepted for symptomatic patients, but prognostic determinants remain poorly defined. This study aimed to synthesize the available surgical literature on ISCH, through a systematic review of published individual patient data (IPD), and to identify clinical, anatomical, and intraoperative factors associated with postoperative motor and sensory outcomes. A systematic review of the literature was performed in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251273863). Studies reporting surgically treated cases of ISCH were identified, from database inception to December 2024. Stringent inclusion criteria were applied. For the enrolled patients, demographic, clinical, radiological, surgical, and postoperative outcome variables were harmonized. Postoperative motor and sensory outcomes were dichotomized as improved versus stable or worsened. Associations were explored using univariate and multivariable logistic regression models to identify factors independently associated with neurological outcomes. A total of 154 studies were included, providing published IPD for 285 surgically treated patients. The cohort consisted predominantly of middle-aged individuals with a slight female predominance, and Brown-Séquard syndrome represented the most frequent neurological presentation. Dural patch reconstruction and primary dural closure were adopted in 68.8% and 31.2% of patients, respectively. Overall, postoperative motor and sensory improvement were observed in 79.2% and 63% of patients, respectively. No significant association was found between dural patch adoption and postoperative motor or sensory improvement. Multivariable logistic regression identified preoperative paraparesis/plegia as independently associated with both motor and sensory stableness or worsened function (p = 0.041; p = 0.014, respectively). The presence of a posterior arachnoid cyst was independently associated with a higher probability of stable/worsened motor outcome (p = 0.033). Duplication of dura mater was associated with a lower probability of stable/worsened sensory outcome (p = 0.036), while dural patch reconstruction was associated with a higher probability of stable/worsened sensory outcome (p = 0.015). Intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring showed significant associations in both motor (p = 0.020) and sensory (p = 0.007). Surgical treatment of ISCH resulted in neurological improvement in a substantial proportion of patients. This IPD analysis identified preoperative neurological impairment and specific anatomical characteristics as factors associated with postoperative recovery, suggesting that advanced neurological deterioration may reduce the probability of functional improvement.These findings should be regarded as exploratory and underscore the need for prospective studies with standardized outcome assessment to refine surgical decision-making in ISCH.

title: Improving the fairness and robustness of deep learning classification models through bias mitigation and post hoc calibration.
journal: International journal of computer assisted radiology and surgery
abstract: The goal of this study was to enhance the fairness and clinical applicability of deep learning models for classifying Alzheimer's disease from structural MRI scans. To achieve this, we addressed two key challenges: age-related bias and unreliable probability estimates. Specifically, we investigated in-processing debiasing strategies to achieve age-invariant predictions while preserving diagnostic accuracy. We also systematically evaluated post hoc calibration methods to improve the reliability, interpretability, and clinical usefulness of predicted probabilities across diverse patient populations. Structural MRI data from three independent cohorts (ADNI, AIBL, and DELCODE) were preprocessed using a standardized pipeline. Age-related bias was addressed using two in-processing strategies, adversarial training (CF-Net) and GLM-based feature residualization (PMDN), implemented in a shared 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) framework. Additionally, post hoc calibration was performed using four regression methods: logistic, probit, isotonic, and Bayesian binning. We evaluated model performance, fairness, and calibration using classification as well as calibration-specific metrics. PMDN achieved the best overall performance, with higher balanced accuracy (0.71) and improved calibration (Brier ≈ 0.22), showing substantially reduced variability compared to baseline and CF-Net. PMDN effectively removed age-related bias, achieving near-zero age prediction correlation; CF-Net, however, showed only partial and unstable debiasing. Post hoc calibration further improved probability reliability, with nonparametric methods (isotonic regression and Bayesian binning) yielding the lowest calibration errors (MCE ≈ 0.21-0.24). This study shows that, although deep learning models achieve similar classification performance, they differ significantly in terms of calibration, stability, and fairness. PMDN provides more consistent and effective age bias mitigation than the CF-Net approach, particularly in clinically relevant subgroups. Post hoc calibration improves probability reliability further, with nonparametric methods achieving the best calibration.

title: A Review of the Molecular Evidence for Near-Infrared Light in Astrocyte-Mediated Neurorehabilitation.
abstract: Near-infrared (NIR) light represents a promising, noninvasive therapeutic for neurological disorders, predicated on its capacity to modulate astrocyte function. As the primary glial population in the central nervous system, astrocytes are indispensable for maintaining neuronal homeostasis, regulating glutamate metabolism, and supporting metabolic energetics. This review synthesizes recent advancements in NIR-driven neurorehabilitation, elucidating the molecular signaling cascades and transduction pathways activated within the astrocytic network. We specifically examine translational applications across preclinical and clinical models of stroke, Alzheimer's disease, epilepsy, and psychiatric disorders. Furthermore, we evaluate how the integration of optogenetic tools and nanomaterials has refined NIR therapies, establishing a foundation for high-precision neurology. Given the rising demand for nonsurgical interventions, this review provides a timely framework for the next generation of photobiomodulation and neural modulation strategies.

title: Autosomal recessive axonal neuropathy with neuromyotonia in a paediatric patient - a case based review.
abstract: Autosomal recessive axonal neuropathy with neuromyotonia (ARAN-NM) is a distinct clinical and genetic entity within the hereditary peripheral neuropathies (HPN), caused by recessive loss-of-function mutations in the histidine triad nucleotide binding protein 1 (HINT1) gene. We report the case of a 13-year-old girl presenting with gait impairment and progressive motor weakness starting at the age of 6, with delayed muscle relaxation after a strong voluntary contraction, which developed later in the course. Electrophysiological studies showed axonal motor polyneuropathy and neuromyotonic discharges. Molecular analysis revealed a homozygous, pathogenic variant, c.110G > C (p.Arg37Pro) in HINT1. This case emphasises the elusive nature of ARAN-NM in children, whose clinical presentation is not distinctly characteristic at onset.

title: Valorization of Beetroot and Watermelon by-Products as Functional Ingredients Targeting Nitric Oxide Pathways: Implications for Cardiovascular Health.
abstract: Food loss and waste represent major challenges for food systems, while fruit and vegetable by-products generated during processing are underused sources of bioactive compounds with potential applications in functional food development. The present review aims to examine the valorization of beetroot and watermelon by-products as functional ingredients associated with nitric oxide (NO) bioavailability, vascular function, and cardiovascular health. Given that impaired NO signaling is a hallmark of endothelial dysfunction and cardiometabolic disease, nutritional strategies capable of modulating NO-related pathways are of growing interest. Beetroot by-products, including peels and pomace, contain betalains, phenolic compounds, dietary fiber, and other constituents of potential functional relevance. However, nitrate content is rarely measured in these materials, and direct evidence that their consumption increases nitrate bioavailability or improves vascular function is currently lacking. Their proposed contribution to the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway is therefore based mainly on evidence from conventional nitrate-rich beetroot products. In contrast, watermelon rind is a natural source of L-citrulline, which is bioavailable after ingestion and may support NO production through the citrulline-arginine-eNOS pathway. Human studies have demonstrated the bioavailability of L-citrulline derived from watermelon rind, while studies using a microencapsulated rind juice providing 4 g of L-citrulline have reported improvements in conduit artery endothelial function. Antioxidant compounds present in these by-products may also help limit oxidative degradation of NO, although this effect has not been directly demonstrated. Beetroot and watermelon by-products are linked to distinct pathways of NO generation but are currently supported by different levels of evidence. Future studies should quantify nitrate in beetroot by-products and L-citrulline in watermelon rind, including in the corresponding final food products, and evaluate changes in circulating nitrate, nitrite, and amino acids together with vascular function in well-controlled clinical studies.

title: Targeting health-related quality of life issues not found with functional outcome measures a year after aneurysm subarachnoid hemorrhage in a Swedish national cohort.
abstract: Outcome after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) is often devastating with life time issues also for independent survivors. We aimed to identify health related quality of life (HRQoL) issues in this favorable functional outcome group compared to a sex and age matched general population. We have analyzed data from 634 Swedish aSAH patients from a national prospective study ranging between 2014 and 2018. One year after ictus, functional outcome was analyzed using Glasgow Outcome Scale Extended (GOSE) and HRQoL assessed by Euro-quality of life-5 dimensions-3 levels (EQ-5D-3L). Favorable GOSE (5-8) were found in 471 patients. Age- and sex-matched populations were created by published data from a cross-sectional cohort of 32,597 people living in Stockholm County in 2006. Odds ratios (ORs) for rating a specific EQ-5D-3L level were calculated for each domain. Significance was set at α = 0.001. Patients reported less mobility problems than the matched general population (9.6% vs 14.7%; OR 0.62 p = 0.002). However, with usual activities significantly more difficulties with moderate, (24.0% vs 10.9%; OR 2.58, p < .001) and any problems (27.0% vs 12.5%; OR 2.58, p < .001) were reported. More issues with extreme anxiety/depression were also reported ((5.3% vs 2.8%; OR 1.94; p = 0.002). Unfavorable GOSE patients were doing worse than the matched population in all levels and dimensions measured (Online Resource 1, 2, 3 and 4). Although patients with favorable functional outcome report good or better mobility compared to their age and sex matched general population, they have significantly more issues with usual activities a year after aSAH more extreme issues with anxiety/depression were also reported To our knowledge, this is the first time EQ-5D-3L data is compared in a national group of aSAH patients with favorable functional outcome to a sex and age matched general population.

title: From Aerosol to Epithelium: An Integrated Clinical, Pathologic, and Mechanistic Review of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaporizer Use and Pulmonary Disease.
abstract: The prevalence of cannabis and nicotine vaporizer use appears to be increasing, but their effects on the respiratory system are incompletely elucidated. This review brings together clinical, pathologic, and molecular knowledge describing airway disease, acute lung injury syndromes, and structural lung injury resulting from nicotine and cannabis vaporizer use. We describe consistent epidemiologic associations of nicotine vaporizer use with obstructive lung disease, bronchitis, emphysema, and constrictive bronchiolitis; cannabis vaporizer use is more frequently associated with acute lung injury and airway disease symptoms. At a molecular level, nicotinic receptor activation drives collagen deposition, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and impaired mucociliary clearance; cannabinoid receptor activation has effects on airway inflammation, epithelial integrity, and immune cell function. Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction likely mediate effects of nicotine and cannabis vaporizer exposure through receptor-independent mechanisms. Use of nicotine and cannabis vaporizers affects clinical pulmonary disease through a variety of converging molecular and cellular mechanisms in the respiratory epithelium. Significant knowledge gaps remain, particularly with regard to molecular investigations of cannabis vaporizer use and dual nicotine-cannabis vaporizer use. Future investigations integrating molecular mechanisms of disease with clinical and histopathologic outcomes are necessary to better characterize the effects of these increasingly impactful public health risks.

title: Italian adaptation of international recommendations for the management of restless legs syndrome: A consensus statement by the scientific committee of RLS-Italia.
journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
abstract: Recent international recommendations have substantially changed the management of restless legs syndrome (RLS), emphasizing systematic iron assessment, earlier use of iron therapy and α2δ ligands, and greater caution with chronic dopaminergic treatment because of augmentation. Their implementation requires adaptation to national healthcare organization, regulatory indications, reimbursement, and access to specialist services. The Scientific Committee of RLS-Italia conducted a structured, non-Delphi consensus process based on the 2025 American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline and systematic review, the 2026 RLS Foundation algorithm, the World Sleep Society partial endorsement, and selected supporting evidence. Successive drafts were circulated, discussed, and approved by all authors. The proposed Italian framework prioritizes clinical diagnosis, exclusion of mimics, correction of exacerbating factors, systematic assessment of iron status, and iron treatment when indicated. α2δ ligands are preferred for most adults with chronic persistent RLS, whereas dopamine agonists should be restricted to selected patients and monitored for augmentation. Refractory or augmented disease should be managed by clinicians with specific RLS expertise, with consideration of intravenous iron, opioids, or device-based treatment. Dipyridamole is not included in the standard pathway, and periodic limb movement disorder should not be diagnosed or treated solely on the basis of polysomnographic findings. This consensus statement provides a nationally coherent framework that can support regional implementation through locally appropriate organizational and clinical protocols.

title: Delays in treatment escalation after failure in multiple sclerosis: the role of therapy type and healthcare system.
journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
abstract: Timely treatment optimization after therapeutic failure is essential in multiple sclerosis (MS), particularly when escalation to high-efficacy therapies (HET) is required. However, real-world delays in treatment initiation remain poorly characterized. To evaluate time to treatment initiation after therapeutic failure in MS according to treatment type and healthcare coverage. We conducted a retrospective observational study using a real-world registry of patients with relapsing-remitting MS. The first treatment switch due to failure per patient was analyzed. The primary outcome was time from failure identification to initiation of subsequent therapy. Treatments were classified as HET or non-HET and healthcare coverage as public, social security, or private. Multivariable analysis used linear regression with log-transformed time, expressed as time ratios (TR). A total of 288 patients were included. Median time to treatment initiation was 142.0 days (IQR 89.0-247.0). Stratified analyses revealed different patterns across healthcare systems. The longest median time to HET initiation was observed with private insurance (211.0 days), whereas the largest within-system difference between HET and non-HET was observed in the public system (165.0 vs. 66.0 days). In multivariable analysis, the HET coefficient was associated with longer time to initiation (TR 3.8, 95% CI 2.5-5.5; p < 0.001), with a significant HET × public system interaction (TR 1.4, 95% CI 1.0-2.1;p = 0.04). Treatment initiation delays after therapeutic failure were substantial and varied according to treatment category and healthcare coverage. These findings highlight the need to better understand barriers between treatment decisions and effective therapy initiation.

title: Gramicidin A attenuates oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, DNA damage, and inflammation in 6-OHDA-induced SH-SY5Y cells.
abstract: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are major contributors to neurodegenerative diseases, and this study investigated the protective potential of Gramicidin A in a 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA)-induced SH-SY5Y cellular injury model relevant to Parkinson's disease (PD). Following the 3-(4,5-Dimethyl-2-thiazolyl)- 2,5-diphenyl-2H-tetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay to determine the appropriate Gramicidin A concentration, cells were evaluated for oxidative stress parameters, including reactive oxygen species (ROS), total antioxidant status (TAS), total oxidant status (TOS), oxidative stress index (OSI), malondialdehyde (MDA), reduced glutathione (GSH), and glutathione peroxidase (GPx), as well as mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), the oxidative DNA damage marker 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), and inflammatory stress markers including interleukin-6 (IL-6), IL-8, and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β). Exposure to 6-OHDA significantly reduced cell viability, increased ROS production, and disrupted oxidative balance (p < 0.0001). In contrast, both pre- and post-treatment with Gramicidin A reduced ROS levels, improved TAS, TOS, and OSI values, decreased MDA levels, increased GSH levels, and modulated GPx activity (p < 0.0001) in SH-SY5Y cells. Gramicidin A treatment also modulated the JC-10 red/green fluorescence ratio, suggesting changes in MMP, decreased 8-OHdG levels, and a significant reduction in 6-OHDA-induced elevations in IL-6, IL-8, and TGF-β levels in SH-SY5Y cells (p < 0.0001). These findings suggest that Gramicidin A attenuates 6-OHDA-induced cellular injury in SH-SY5Y cells by modulating oxidative stress, mitochondrial membrane potential-related changes, oxidative DNA damage, and inflammatory stress responses.

title: Imaging findings of sacroiliac joint degeneration are prevalent in asymptomatic adults: a systemic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: The purpose of this study is to determine the prevalence of imaging findings of sacroiliac joint (SIJ) degeneration in asymptomatic adults. All studies reporting the prevalence of cross-sectional imaging findings of SIJ degeneration in asymptomatic adults through May 2026 were included. Pooled prevalence and 95% confidence intervals were calculated using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed with I2 and Cochran's Q. Age and sex subgroup analyses were performed. Seventeen studies (3873 patients) were included. Any feature of degeneration was observed in 71.1% of patients (95% CI [25.8, 94.6]) with significant heterogeneity among studies (I2 = 96%, p < .01). Osteophyte formation was most prevalent (68.4%; 95% CI [37.5, 88.7], I2 = 92%), followed by joint space narrowing (45.2%; 95% CI [9.8, 86.3], I2 = 99%), subchondral sclerosis (39.1%; 95% CI [11.7, 75.7], I2 = 96%), vacuum phenomenon (14.3%; 95% CI [6.4, 28.7], I2 = 94%), subchondral cyst formation (5.5%; 95% CI [3.0, 9.9], I2 = 59%), erosions (5.0%; 95% CI [2.1, 11.2], I2 = 86%), and joint ankylosis (2.8%; 95% CI [1.2, 6.5], I2 = 66%). There was a correlation between age and osteophytosis, subchondral sclerosis, and vacuum phenomenon. Our study reveals a high prevalence of imaging findings related to SIJ degeneration in asymptomatic adults, which may have a connection with age in several findings. These findings emphasize the importance of correlating imaging with clinical symptoms and physical examination findings in the evaluation of low back pain. Findings should be interpreted with caution because confidence intervals were wide and between-study heterogeneity was high, reflecting differences in imaging modality, lesion definitions, and patient categorization.

title: Re: Brodie et al.: Clinical Outcomes of a Prosthetic Capsular Bag for Scleral Fixation of an Intraocular Lens in Eyes without Capsular Support (Ophthalmology. 2026;133:965-970).
Slow-wave sleep selectively amplifies network signatures of the presumed epileptogenic zone in focal epilepsy.
abstract: Slow-wave sleep increases interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) and seizures in focal epilepsy, but how sleep stages reshape epileptogenic tissue remains unclear. We assessed whether sleep stages selectively modulate network properties of the presumed epileptogenic zone (pEZ) relative to irritative (IZ) and non-involved (NIZ) zones. We studied 22 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy undergoing pre-surgical intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG). IED-free resting-state epochs spanned four vigilance stages: wakefulness, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep stages 2 and 3, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Spectral power, functional connectivity, graph-theoretic indices, and the 1/f exponent were quantified across seven frequency bands. Sleep stage and zone interactions were tested using permutation testing. pEZ electrodes were classified using elastic net logistic regression with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. NREM3 selectively amplified within-pEZ gamma-band synchrony beyond surrounding zones (pEZ-NIZ: d=1.204, P=0.027). pEZ local efficiency and betweenness centrality rose in beta1 and gamma bands versus wakefulness. The aperiodic exponent steepened within the IZ versus NIZ during NREM3 and NREM2 (d =1.452 and 0.87, P < 0.001 and P=0.015). A three-feature classifier (NREM3 aperiodic exponent, beta2 connectivity, gamma local efficiency) localised the pEZ without ictal recordings (median AUC 0.859 pEZ vs. non-pEZ). Slow-wave sleep selectively unmasks pEZ network properties via amplified power, synchrony and hub topology. NREM3-derived multimodal features may complement conventional pre-surgical biomarkers. Prospective validation in larger cohorts is needed to determine whether these markers improve surgical planning and outcome prediction.

title: Spatial Neighborhood Construction and NICHES Connectomics for Differential Ligand-Receptor Analysis in Fibrotic Human Lung.
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables measurement of gene expression within intact tissue architecture, yet most analytical workflows emphasize cell-type classification over cellular interaction. Workflows that do infer intercellular signaling typically aggregate inferred interactions across clusters, regions, or spots, and fix neighborhood definitions, ligand-receptor (LR) databases, and scoring functions that users cannot easily inspect or change. The unmet need is therefore an analysis workflow that preserves signaling inference at the resolution of individual cell-cell pairs, constrains candidate interactions using measured physical distance, and exposes every modeling choice as a user-set parameter. Here, we describe a computational protocol that meets these requirements by inferring LR signaling at cell-cell pair resolution, grounded in physical tissue space, from imaging-based spatial transcriptomics data. The workflow defines spatial neighborhoods and constructs a directed connectomics graph in which edges represent the set of inferred LR interactions between cells. Using the NICHES (Niche Interactions and Communication Heterogeneity in Extracellular Signaling) package, three complementary representations are derived: a Cell-to-Cell (C2C) edge-level connectome, a Cell-to-Neighborhood (C2N) outgoing signaling summary, and a Neighborhood-to-Cell (N2C) incoming signaling summary. A parallel Neighborhood Composition assay characterizes the local tissue architecture of the spatial neighborhoods. The framework is modular and tunable: users may adjust neighborhood definitions, select alternative LR databases, and modify scoring and aggregation methods. These node- and edge-aligned data layers support visualization, clustering, and differential analysis of spatially organized signaling patterns. Applied to fibrotic lung tissue, the workflow segregates architecturally defined neighborhoods and identifies differential LR mechanisms that distinguish fibrotic regions from surrounding tissue. This protocol provides a reproducible framework for studying spatially organized intercellular communication across tissues and disease contexts.

title: Clinical Improvement Following Multimodal Treatment in Depersonalization-Derealization Disorder: A Case Report.
abstract: Depersonalization-derealization disorder (DPD) is characterized by persistent or recurrent detachment from the self or the surrounding environment with preserved reality testing. Because established treatment evidence remains limited, individualized therapeutic strategies are often required. This report describes a patient with derealization, emotional blunting, poor memory, slowed reactions, and impaired attention. Psychiatric evaluation showed marked depersonalization-derealization symptoms, with a Cambridge Depersonalization Scale (CDS) score of 147, a 24-item Hamilton Depression (HAMD-24) Rating Scale score of 8, a 14-item Hamilton Anxiety (HAMA-14) Rating Scale score of 5, and a MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery (MCCB) composite T-score of 49. The patient underwent a stepwise multimodal treatment approach that included transcranial direct current stimulation, pharmacotherapy with duloxetine and tandospirone, duloxetine dose optimization, lamotrigine augmentation and titration, and later gradual medication tapering under follow-up monitoring. Clinical improvement was observed during longitudinal assessment. This case highlights the practical value of a monitored, sequential, and multimodal treatment strategy for a patient with DPD. Although the findings are limited to a single case, the observed temporal association between intervention and improvement provides a hypothesis-generating clinical observation and supports the need for systematic studies of multimodal treatment approaches in DPD.

title: Response to "Comment on 'Cognitive & Behavioral Assessment Toolbox (CBAT): An open-source platform supporting experiments in computational psychiatry'".
abstract: This article relates to Response to "Comment on 'Cognitive & Behavioral Assessment Toolbox (CBAT): An open-source platform supporting experiments in computational psychiatry'".

title: From spatial bias to temporal integration: Anorthoscopy neutralizes pseudoneglect.
abstract: The present study investigated interaction between spatio-temporal integration under conditions of sensory impoverishment, "anorthoscopic viewing", and the lateralized spatial biases, such as pseudoneglect, aiming to clarify whether such asymmetries originate from early perceptual mechanisms or from intrinsic properties of high-level neural representations. A 64-object array, organized in 2 × 6, was presented in two experiments: (1) anorthoscopic viewing (stimuli were presented sliding behind a static aperture) and (2) the whole condition. Participants were asked to recall as many items as possible for each trial in both experiments. Results demonstrate a robust pseudoneglect effect in Experiment 2, characterized by significantly higher recall for items on the left side of the arrays compared to the right. Pseudoneglect was absent in the anorthoscopic condition. Notably, while the recall of left-sided items decreased during the anorthoscopic session, performance for right-sided objects remained statistically stable across both experiments. These findings indicate that anorthoscopic procedure doesn't impair performance through generic degradation or excessive cognitive load. Because attentional and mnemonic factors interact, these results should be interpreted as reflecting an interplay between the two mechanisms. Accordingly, we suggest that pseudoneglect is not an intrinsic property of static internal mental representations, but a dynamic consequence of active visual scanning.

title: Neurofilaments in cerebrospinal fluid and/or serum as a possible biomarker of pediatric spinal muscular atrophy.
abstract: BackgroundSpinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a severe, genetically determined neuromuscular disorder characterised by progressive muscle weakness resulting from motor neuron degeneration. Although therapies such as nusinersen have altered disease trajectories, objective biomarkers for treatment monitoring remain lacking. Neurofilament proteins, particularly phosphorylated neurofilament heavy chain (pNFH), are promising candidates for this role.ObjectivesTo evaluate pNFH levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and serum as potential biomarkers for monitoring treatment response to nusinersen in paediatric patients with SMA.MethodsThis two-center observational study involved 56 SMA patients (types I-III) treated with nusinersen and 30 age-matched controls. pNFH concentrations in CSF and serum were measured at predefined intervals using ELISA kits. Motor function was assessed with CHOP INTEND, HFMSE, or MFM scales at baseline and after 3, 6, and 12 months. Mixed linear regression modeling evaluated changes in neurofilament levels and motor function.ResultsBaseline pNFH levels in both CSF and serum were significantly higher in SMA patients compared to controls. Following nusinersen therapy, pNFH levels decreased significantly in both compartments, especially in the first 6 months. Younger patients had higher initial serum pNFH levels. A significant correlation was found between CSF and serum pNFH concentration. An association between pNFH levels and motor scores was observed.ConclusionspNFH levels in CSF and serum show potential as objective biomarkers for monitoring the initial treatment response in paediatric SMA. Longitudinal changes are more informative than single measurements. Further validation in larger cohorts and using more sensitive methods is warranted.

title: Social Support Modifies the Pain-Disability Relationship in Degenerative Spine Disease: Evidence From the PROGRES Study.
abstract: Low back pain from degenerative spine disease is the main contributor to years lived with disability globally. Although social support is a multifaceted construct with both health-promoting and potentially deleterious effects on chronic pain, whether perceived social support modifies the pain-disability relationship in lumbar degenerative spine disease remains unclear. We hypothesised that social support level would modify the pain-disability association, with distinct predictor patterns of disability emerging for low- versus high-support patients. In this cross-sectional analysis of baseline data from the PROGRES cohort study, 156 pre-operative patients with lumbar degenerative disease (mean age 60.0 years; 58.3% female) completed validated measures of pain (Visual Analog Scale [VAS] for radicular and axial pain, supplemented by the pain/discomfort item of the EuroQol EQ-5D-5L [EQ-5D pain]), disability (Oswestry Disability Index [ODI]), health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L), and perceived social support (Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support [MSPSS]). Participants were stratified by median MSPSS score into low- (n = 83) and high-support (n = 73) groups. The primary outcome was the between-group difference in pain-disability correlations, tested with Fisher's z-transformation and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. The robustness of dichotomisation was confirmed using moderation analysis with MSPSS as a continuous variable. After FDR correction, the correlation between EQ-5D pain severity and the ODI daily-activities item was significantly stronger in the high-support group than in the low-support group (ρ = 0.69 vs. 0.25; Δρ = 0.44; PFDR = 0.005). Multiple regression models explained more variance of disability in the high-support group (R2 = 31.5%) than in the low-support group (R2 = 16.6%). Depression was a significant predictor of disability in both groups; in the low-support group, it was the sole significant predictor (p = 0.037), whereas in the high-support group, radicular (leg) pain emerged as the dominant predictor (B = 1.45; β = 0.50; p < 0.001) alongside depression (B = 1.83; β = 0.31; p = 0.007). Higher perceived social support showed a small positive correlation with radicular pain intensity (ρ = +0.18; p = 0.026), with no significant association with axial pain. Perceived social support appears to influence which factors are most strongly associated with disability rather than uniformly buffering against it. The positive pain-support correlation, restricted to radicular pain, is consistent with operant models of social support in chronic pain, in which clinically unambiguous symptoms may preferentially mobilise support. Brief screening of perceived social support may help inform individualised treatment planning in degenerative spine disease.

title: Lymphocytosis as a biomarker for natalizumab treatment response in multiple sclerosis: The link with anti-drug antibodies.
abstract: Natalizumab is a high-efficacy therapy drug for multiple sclerosis that inhibits lymphocyte migration into the central nervous system, increasing lymphocyte counts in the peripheral blood. Anti-drug antibody responses may limit drug efficacy, but current guidance recommends anti-drug antibody testing only after evidence of 'reduced efficacy'. To assess the lack of relative lymphocytosis as a biomarker of anti-drug antibody responses. Lymphocyte counts and immunogenicity data from the pivotal AFFIRM clinical trial (n = 627 natalizumab vs n = 315 placebo) and real-world data from the Cardiff MS register (n = 185) were analysed to assess the relationship between lymphocyte counts, anti-drug antibody responses, drug levels and disease activity. Natalizumab treatment induced an absolute change in lymphocyte counts by week 12 (1.40 ± 0.92 vs -0.05 ± 0.62 × 109 cells/L in natalizumab vs placebo; p < 0.0001) that was absent in the persistent anti-drug antibody group (-0.12 ± 0.60 × 109 cells/L). Increases in lymphocyte counts by ⩾ 0.8 × 109 cells/L from the baseline discriminated individuals without anti-drug antibody responses with high sensitivity (≥ 84%) and specificity (≥ 91%). The absence of relative lymphocytosis is associated with anti-drug antibody responses and may provide a simple biomarker to prompt anti-drug antibody testing before disease breakthrough occurs.

title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) as a COVID-19 Complication: A Multicenter Study Conducted Throughout the 2-Year Pandemic.
abstract: Several studies have been published on the coexistence of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and COVID-19, raising the question of whether SARS-CoV-2 plays a role in GBS pathogenesis or is just a coincidence. In this research, we discuss GBS characteristics in COVID-19 patients during the pandemic. This cross-sectional, multi-center study was performed on patients who were hospitalized in one of two GBS referral hospitals in Isfahan Providence between March 2020 to March 2022. All confirmed GBS and COVID-19 patients with no other known risk factor for GBS and no more than 28 days of COVID-19 treatment were entered into the trial. Totally, 45 patients were collected. The most prevalent EDX pattern was AIDP (57.8%). As compared to demyelinating injuries, axonal injuries were significantly more associated with lung involvement (P value: 0.022), higher GBS disability score (P value: 0.034), poorer response to treatment (P value: 0.021), higher serum inflammatory level, and older onset (P value: 0.013). The average period between the onset of COVID-19 and the onset of GBS symptoms was 18.07 ± 9.88 days. 46.3% of patients developed GBS within the first two weeks of COVID-19, a condition known as a para-infection. The axonal injury was significantly more prevalent in these individuals (P value: 0.045). An earlier onset of neurological symptoms and para-infection conditions is associated with an increase in the frequency of axonal-type variations and, as a result, a poor prognosis. The majority of evidence in COVID-19-related GBS patients points to an autoimmune process.

title: Lipid Nanoparticle-Mediated Antifungal and Immunomodulatory Therapy for Neuromycoses.
abstract: Neuromycoses, fungal infections affecting the central nervous system (CNS), cause approximately 112,000 deaths annually, representing 19% of AIDS-related deaths globally. Conventional antifungal drugs are limited by poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, systemic toxicity, and increasing drug resistance. Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as promising vehicles for enhancing antifungal efficacy while modulating immune responses. Thus, this comprehensive review synthesizes current knowledge on LNPs as vehicles for antifungal immune modulators, including their design principles, drug delivery mechanisms, physiological interactions, translational potential, and roadmap for next-generation precision medicine approaches to treating neuromycoses. A comprehensive narrative review of original studies on LNP-based approaches for neuromycoses was conducted. The literature was synthesized using a structured evidence table encompassing six studies published between 2019 and 2026, including one randomized clinical trial in adults, one case report, one in vitro study, two animal studies, and one study incorporating both in vitro and in vivo approaches. Original research studies were prioritized, while reviews, commentaries, and editorials were excluded. This review shows four principal findings: (1) LNP formulations achieved mean fungicidal activity of 0.402 log1 0 CFU/mL/day, non-inferior to intravenous amphotericin B, with 18-week survival and reduced toxicity compared to intravenous formulations; (2) LNPs cross the BBB with limited or no systemic toxicity while enabling intracellular trafficking through optimization of lipid composition and surface chemistry; (3) RMT demonstrates high specificity affected by variability in receptor expression, while AMT and TMT operate through distinct mechanisms with their own potential off-target effects; and (4) encapsulation reduces nephrotoxicity and hepatotoxicity compared to free antifungal drugs, with amphotericin B-loaded NLC showing reduced nephrotoxicity in vitro compared to conventional formulations. These findings highlight the potential of LNP-based antifungal delivery and the need for further clinical validation before broader clinical translation.

title: Alternative and Synergistic Strategies Against Antibiotic-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus in Clinical and Environmental Settings.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) poses a serious global health threat, undermining treatment outcomes and necessitating the development of innovative therapeutic strategies. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major contributor to this burden, with increasing prevalence in hospitals, contaminated food, and environmental sources. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic further intensified S. aureus resistance due to widespread antibiotic misuse. Biofilm formation, which facilitates the horizontal transfer of resistance genes such as mecA (methicillin resistance gene A), plays a central role in the development of resistance. To counteract antibiotic-resistant S. aureus, alternative approaches have emerged, including antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), photodynamic therapy (PDT), and drug repurposing guided by artificial intelligence (AI). Cutting-edge technologies such as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-CRISPR-associated protein 13a (Cas13a)-based gene editing and engineered bacteriophages offer promising avenues for targeting resistant strains. Natural compounds such as thymol and chlorogenic acid (CGA) have also shown potential in reducing resistance and inhibiting biofilm formation. Effective management of AMR requires strengthened antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs), robust surveillance systems, and public health measures such as proper hand hygiene and environmental sanitation. Combining antibiotic adjuvants (AAs) with existing antibiotics and leveraging bioactive peptides (BAPs) can enhance antibiotic efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR), extensively drug-resistant (XDR), and pan-drug-resistant (PDR) S. aureus. This review investigates the prevalence and resistance mechanisms of S. aureus in clinical, food, and environmental contexts, explores promising alternative therapies, and emphasizes the urgent need for global antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) and sustainable intervention strategies.

title: Clinical and Genetic Spectrum of VPS13A Disease Across India: A Retrospective Multicentre Genetically Confirmed Cohort.
journal: Tremor and other hyperkinetic movements (New York, N.Y.)
abstract: To characterize the geographic and molecular spectrum of genetically confirmed VPS13A disease across India and examine patterns of delay to tertiary evaluation. We conducted a multicentre retrospective study across eight tertiary movement disorder centres in India. Clinical, investigational, genetic, treatment, and follow-up data were collected. Eighteen unrelated patients from eight tertiary centres were included. Chorea was the most common initial manifestation (10/18), and 8/18 patients were evaluated more than five years after symptom onset. Longer intervals to tertiary evaluation were descriptively more frequent among patients with non-choreic presentations, particularly seizures. Twenty-three distinct VPS13A variants were identified, predominantly loss-of-function variants, including apparently novel variants and two variants recurring in unrelated patients. VPS13A disease in this multicentre Indian cohort demonstrated substantial molecular heterogeneity, including apparently novel and recurrent variants. Longer intervals to tertiary evaluation were descriptively more frequent among patients with non-choreic presentations, particularly those with seizures, highlighting that clinicians need to maintain a high degree of suspicion for VPS13A even in such presentations.

title: Autophagy-Modulating Nanomedicine for Glioma: Delivery Barriers, Lysosomal Interactions, and a Flux-Resolved Translational Decision Framework.
abstract: Glioma nanomedicine is constrained by linked delivery and pharmacodynamic barriers: nanoscale systems must traverse heterogeneous blood-brain barrier (BBB) and blood-brain tumor barrier (BBTB) interfaces and achieve interpretable intracellular effects in tumor cells. Autophagy is a therapeutically relevant but context-dependent axis. However, similar changes in static autophagy markers, vesicular staining, or ultrastructure can reflect productive autophagy induction (ie, increased autophagic flux with successful lysosomal cargo degradation), blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, lysosomal dysfunction, or secondary cytotoxic stress. This ambiguity is amplified for nanomedicines because their physicochemical properties can independently shape autophagy-related readouts. Here, we frame autophagy-modulating nanomedicine for glioma as both a delivery challenge and a problem of translational interpretation, covering bioactive nanomaterials, nanocarriers, and multimodal platforms. We organize the field around an integrated framework linking BBB/BBTB access, intracellular trafficking, interpretation of autophagic flux, and translational readiness. We use structured evidence grading to distinguish flux-resolved, functionally validated mechanisms from marker-based or indirect inferences. This framework distinguishes mechanistically supported findings from provisional interpretations and defines the evidence required for translational progression.

title: Metabolomic and lipidomic signatures of Helicobacter pylori infection: Unveiling biochemical pathways associated with neurodegeneration.
abstract: Our study employed an integrated lipidomics and metabolomics approach to elucidate Helicobacter pylori-driven metabolic perturbations along the gut-brain axis. H. pylori infection was established in gastric epithelial (AGS) cells, and the resulting conditioned media (secretome) was collected and exposed to neuronal (IMR-32) cells. Gastric, neuronal, and secretome samples were then harvested for the extraction of metabolites and lipids. Comprehensive molecular profiling was performed using high-resolution LC-MS/HRMS. The acquired data were analysed through lipidomics and metabolomics pipelines to identify significantly altered metabolites and lipid species. Subsequent statistical and pathway enrichment analyses uncovered dysregulated metabolic pathways. Finally, network-based interaction analysis integrated disease-associated metabolites to identify key molecular hubs potentially linking H. pylori infection to neuronal metabolic dysfunction and neurodegenerative processes.

title: Excessive Yawning During Escitalopram Therapy in a Rwandan Woman with Co-Morbid Depression and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder: A Case Report.
abstract: Excessive yawning is an uncommon but recognized adverse effect of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). Although generally benign, it may cause distress and may be mistaken for a symptom of psychiatric or neurological illness. Case reports and pharmacovigilance data have linked escitalopram to yawning, sometimes in a dose-dependent manner. To our knowledge, this is one of the first reported cases of escitalopram-associated yawning in Rwanda. We describe a 44-year-old woman from rural Rwanda who presented with a severe depressive episode and comorbid post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Three days after starting escitalopram 10 mg daily, she reported markedly increased yawning, approximately six episodes every 15 minutes throughout the day, while her sleep and mood had begun to improve slightly. Medical and neurological causes, sleep-related causes and concurrent short-term diazepam use were considered and judged unlikely. The Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale score was 5, indicating a probable adverse drug reaction. Escitalopram was continued because of emerging antidepressant benefit, and the yawning had decreased substantially at the two-week follow-up. This case suggests that yawning occurring early in escitalopram treatment should be recognized as a probable adverse drug reaction. Awareness of this under-reported effect may prevent unnecessary investigations and premature discontinuation of an effective antidepressant.

title: The 23rd AMN Congress | Integrated Pathway Management in Neurotrauma: From ER and ICU to Rehabilitation and Mental Health.
Anxiety and depressive symptoms in patients with acute ischaemic stroke and cognitive dysfunction: a retrospective single-center study.
abstract: Anxiety and depressive symptoms may coexist with cognitive dysfunction after stroke. This study characterized their frequency and severity during acute stroke hospitalization in patients with documented cognitive dysfunction. We conducted a retrospective, single-center study of 95 adults with acute ischaemic stroke (AIS) and cognitive dysfunction in Romania during 2024-2025. Anxiety and depressive symptoms were derived from neuropsychological conclusions and classified as absent/minimal, mild, moderate, or severe. In the main analysis, "elements" and the depression-specific "tendency" were classified as absent/minimal, while hybrid descriptors were assigned to the adjacent higher category. Sensitivity analyses examined alternative allocations. Associations were assessed using the chi-square, Fisher's exact, or Kruskal-Wallis test. Anxiety severity was available for 94 patients and was distributed as follows: 26.6% absent/minimal, 16.0% mild, 50.0% moderate, and 7.4% severe. The severe category derived from "moderate-severe" descriptors. Overall, 73.4% had anxiety of at least mild severity. Depression severity was available for 86 patients, distributed as 74.4% absent/minimal, 17.4% mild, 7.0% moderate, and 1.2% severe; 25.6% had depression of at least mild severity. Under alternative low-level classifications, the anxiety-depression difference at the at-least-mild threshold narrowed from 47.8 to 28.1 and 9.0 percentage points. Anxiety remained more frequent. Sex was associated with both severity distributions. These proportions reflect documented severity rather than prevalence estimates derived from a uniform standardized instrument. Anxiety was more frequently documented and more often reached moderate-or-greater severity than depression. Routine neuropsychological conclusions may provide information on the affective profile during this phase of care. Longitudinal studies should examine affective, cognitive, and functional trajectories during recovery.

title: Coreopsis tinctoria Nutt. Polyphenols Ameliorate CUMS-Induced Depressive Behaviors and Hippocampal Neuronal Damage in Mice.
abstract: Chronic stress-induced mood disturbances have become a prominent public health concern, and dietary polyphenols are emerging as natural nutritional strategies for mood health management. The capitula of Coreopsis tinctoria Nutt. (CCT) are edible flowers rich in polyphenols, but their mood-supporting efficacy remains unclear. This study investigated the effects, mechanisms, and key bioactive constituents of CCT polyphenol extract (CCTE) in a chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) mouse model. High-dose CCTE (1 g/kg) restored sucrose preference from 30.9% ± 4.1% in CUMS mice to 52.0% ± 5.5%, increased week-6 weight gain from 4.7% ± 2.4% to 38.8% ± 5.9% (p < 0.001), and restored open-field rearing, central-area crossings, and residence time to fluoxetine-comparable levels, indicating dose-dependent attenuation of CUMS-induced depressive-like behaviors. It also ameliorated hippocampal neuronal damage, corrected the CUMS-induced 36.7% reduction in serum 5-HT and 44.8% elevation in 5-HIAA, attenuated hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) hyperactivity, particularly reducing elevated CRH, ACTH, and CORT levels, alleviated oxidative stress, and suppressed NLRP3 inflammasome-driven neuroinflammation via NLRP3/NF-κB downregulation. Three flavonoid aglycones-okanin (OKA), isookanin (ISO), taxifolin (TAX)-crossed the blood-brain barrier (free C max 28.45 ± 10.9, 32.74 ± 27.3, 32.04 ± 6.9 ng/g; T max 20-45 min) and inhibited monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A; IC50 38.66 ± 2.45, 48.23 ± 3.12, 47.28 ± 2.98 μmol/L); their equimolar mixture acted synergistically (IC50 18.79 ± 1.67 μmol/L; pargyline 8.71 ± 1.21 μmol/L, p < 0.001). Thus, CCTE ameliorates stress-induced mood disturbances through multi-target regulation and shows potential as a functional food ingredient.

title: Metabolic syndrome in patients diagnosed with affective disorders: a cross-sectional study among inpatients from two Cluj-Napoca psychiatry clinics.
abstract: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is highly prevalent among individuals with affective disorders and contributes substantially to premature cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. However, the relative contribution of demographic characteristics, psychiatric diagnosis, and psychotropic medication to metabolic risk remains incompletely understood. This study investigated the prevalence of MetS and its associated demographic, clinical, and treatment-related factors in hospitalized patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD). A cross-sectional study was conducted in 502 adult psychiatric inpatients diagnosed with MDD or BD. Metabolic syndrome was defined according to the National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel III (NCEP ATP III) criteria. Demographic characteristics, psychiatric diagnosis, metabolic parameters, and psychotropic medication were analyzed. Independent correlates of MetS were identified using multivariable binary logistic regression, excluding variables constituting the diagnostic criteria for MetS to avoid circularity. Metabolic syndrome was identified in 25.4% of the study population. Patients with MetS were significantly older and more frequently female than those without MetS (both p < 0.001). Although bipolar disorder was not significantly associated with MetS in univariate analyses, it became independently associated with MetS after multivariable adjustment (adjusted OR 1.77, 95% CI 1.04-3.02; p = 0.037), together with increasing age (adjusted OR 1.06 per year, 95% CI 1.04-1.08; p < 0.001) and female sex (adjusted OR 1.87, 95% CI 1.18-2.98; p = 0.008). Current psychotropic medication, assessed at the time of hospital admission, was not independently associated with MetS after adjustment for demographic and clinical characteristics. These findings should not be interpreted as evidence against the established long-term metabolic effects of psychotropic medication. Metabolic syndrome represents a common medical comorbidity among hospitalized patients with affective disorders. Increasing age, female sex, and bipolar disorder were independently associated with MetS, whereas current psychotropic medication, assessed cross-sectionally at hospital admission, was not independently associated with metabolic syndrome after adjustment. This finding should be interpreted in the context of unavailable information regarding cumulative treatment exposure, duration, dosage, and previous medication history. These findings support routine metabolic monitoring as an integral component of psychiatric care, particularly among older adults, women, and patients with bipolar disorder.

title: Functional pseudocoarctation after branched arch endograft implantation in a patient with previous type A aortic dissection repair.
Deciphering interventional dynamical causality from non-intervention complex systems.
abstract: Detecting and quantifying causal influence is a focal topic in the fields of science, engineering, and interdisciplinary studies. However, causal studies on non-intervention systems attract much attention but remain extremely challenging. The delay-embedding technique provides a promising approach. In this study, we propose a framework named interventional dynamical causality (IntDC) in contrast to the traditional constructive dynamical causality (ConDC). ConDC, including Granger causality, transfer entropy, and convergence of cross-mapping, measures the causality by constructing a dynamical model without considering interventions. A computational criterion, interventional embedding entropy (IEE), is proposed to measure causal strengths in an interventional manner. IEE is an intervened causal information flow but in the delay-embedding space. Further, the IEE theoretically and numerically enables the deciphering of IntDC solely from observational (non-interventional) time-series data, without requiring any knowledge of dynamical models or real interventions in the considered system. In particular, IEE can be applied to rank causal effects according to their importance and construct causal networks from data. We conducted numerical experiments on logistic dynamics, coupled-Hénon maps, and chaotic neural networks to demonstrate that IEE can find causal edges accurately, eliminate effects of confounding, and quantify causal strength robustly over traditional indices. We also applied IEE to real-world tasks, including estimating neural connectomes of Caenorhabditis elegans, detecting COVID-19 transmission networks in Japan, and investigating regulatory networks surrounding key circadian genes. IEE performed as an accurate and robust tool for causal analyses solely from the observational data. Both the IntDC framework and the IEE algorithm proposed in this study provide an approach to understanding causal influence in diverse non-intervention complex systems.

title: Optimized enrichment of circulating extracellular vesicles from whole blood samples using PROSPR.
journal: Extracellular vesicles and circulating nucleic acids
abstract: Aim: Whole blood constitutes a robust and readily available resource for the identification and characterization of systemically circulating substances. Despite the relevant number of blood specimens archived in biobanks globally, their utilization in extracellular vesicle (EV) research remains considerably underexploited. In this study, we present an optimized PRotein Organic Solvent PRecipitation (PROSPR) workflow, specifically designed for the rapid and standardized enrichment of EVs directly from untreated blood samples. Methods: PROSPR workflow was applied for EV enrichment directly from untreated blood. Comprehensive biophysical characterization was performed using dedicated flow cytometry, tunable resistive pulse sensing, and transmission electron microscopy. In parallel, discovery-driven lipidomics and high-depth proteomics were applied to assess the suitability of PROSPR-derived EVs for advanced systems biology and multi-omics integration. Results: PROSPR consistently yielded highly purified EV preparations that preserved canonical vesicular morphology, structural integrity, and stable ζ-potentials, indicative of intact membrane characteristics. Multi-omics analyses revealed distinct and coordinated lipid-protein signatures uniquely enriched in EV populations derived from whole blood. These signatures predominantly reflected platelet- and mitochondria-associated cargo that was not detectable in corresponding plasma-derived EV fractions, highlighting key molecular features missed by plasma-based EV profiling approaches. Conclusion: Consequently, the optimized PROSPR workflow presented here offers a robust and accessible methodological strategy to fully utilize dormant, archived blood resources within global and national biobanks, thereby enabling comprehensive mechanistic insights and facilitating the discovery of novel diagnostic and prognostic circulating biomarkers.

title: Therapeutic mechanistic framework of mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles in neurodegenerative diseases.
journal: Extracellular vesicles and circulating nucleic acids
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a spectrum of progressive disorders unified by chronic neuroinflammation, oxidative and mitochondrial stress, and accumulation of misfolded proteins that ultimately drive neuronal dysfunction and loss. Despite recurring convergence on these pathogenic processes, therapeutic progress has remained limited, underscoring the need for interventions capable of targeting convergent pathogenic pathways rather than single downstream features. Mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs) have emerged as promising therapeutic candidates through their paracrine actions that modulate inflammatory and cellular stress responses within the nervous system. Increasing evidence indicates that extracellular vesicles released by MSCs (MSC-EVs) are key mediators of these effects, transferring regulatory RNAs, lipids, and proteins that reprogram recipient cells, attenuate neuroinflammatory cascades, and support neuronal survival. MSC-EVs can recapitulate key therapeutic mechanisms of their parent cells and may offer potential advantages in safety, scalability, and delivery across the blood-brain barrier. While MSC-EVs are promising candidates for treating these diseases, the molecular mechanisms underlying their effects are still emerging. In this review, we synthesise evidence from experimental models to develop a mechanistic framework describing how MSC-EVs modulate interconnected regulatory modules that shape neuroinflammation with blood-brain barrier dysfunction, oxidative and mitochondrial stress, and dysregulated proteostasis with loss of neurotrophic support. We further discuss how this modular perspective may inform strategies to mitigate infection-associated neurodegenerative trajectories, with particular attention to post-SARS-CoV-2 neurological sequelae. By integrating these mechanistic insights, this review provides a conceptual foundation for the rational optimisation and bioengineering of MSC-EV-based therapies targeting convergent regulatory pathways in neurodegeneration.

title: Extracellular vesicles for Alzheimer's disease therapy: mechanisms, engineering strategies, and clinical translation.
journal: Extracellular vesicles and circulating nucleic acids
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD), a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, remains a major global health challenge owing to its complex pathogenesis and the presence of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which substantially limits the delivery of effective therapeutics to the brain. Extracellular vesicles (EVs), which exhibit favorable biocompatibility, low immunogenicity, and the potential to cross or bypass the BBB under specific conditions, have emerged as promising therapeutic agents and delivery platforms for AD. This review focuses on the therapeutic potential of EV-based interventions in AD and summarizes recent advances in EV-mediated modulation of AD-related pathological processes, including amyloid-β (Aβ) clearance, tau protein regulation, neuroinflammation suppression, oxidative stress attenuation, and synaptic repair. Although EV-based therapies offer notable advantages, such as targeted BBB penetration and reduced immunogenic responses, their clinical translation remains constrained by safety concerns, including off-target effects, dose-dependent toxicity, and potential disturbances in neuroplasticity. In addition, this review discusses EV engineering strategies aimed at regulating the gut-brain axis (GBA), enhancing brain targeting, and advancing clinical translation. EV-based therapeutic interventions should therefore be developed within a safety-oriented framework supported by rigorous short- and long-term toxicological evaluation. Overall, this review highlights the therapeutic promise of EVs for AD while underscoring the need for rational engineering, standardized characterization, and safety-centered translational strategies to ensure clinical feasibility.

title: Dexmedetomidine as a potential neuroprotective agent against Alzheimer's disease: molecular mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by extracellular deposition of amyloid-β (Aβ), intracellular hyperphosphorylation of microtubule-associated protein tau and chronic neuroinflammation. At present, effective disease-modifying therapies for AD remain limited. Dexmedetomidine (Dex), a highly selective α2-adrenergic receptor agonist, has been reported in recent years to exert significant neuroprotective effects. Accumulating evidence indicates that Dex may ameliorate AD pathology through multiple mechanisms. In terms of Aβ metabolism, Dex reduces Aβ production by downregulating β-site amyloid precursor protein-cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1) expression. With respect to tau pathology, Dex may counteract abnormal tau hyperphosphorylation in AD-related models, although relatively high experimental doses have also been associated with increased tau phosphorylation. Regarding immune regulation, Dex attenuates neuroinflammatory signaling by inhibiting NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome activation and related pro-inflammatory pathways. In addition, Dex modulates neurotrophic support, ferroptosis, autophagic flux, and synaptic homeostasis. These multitarget effects have been observed across heterogeneous preclinical models and dose ranges; however, an AD-specific therapeutic window and long-term safety profile remain to be established. This narrative review synthesizes the available preclinical evidence on the multitarget actions of Dex in AD-related models and critically evaluates dose dependence, pharmacokinetic and safety considerations, and current translational limitations.

title: Correlation of blood biomarkers with microstructural brain injury in survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
abstract: In-hospital mortality among resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients remains high. Identifying patients who will benefit from intensive care while avoiding prolonged, potentially unnecessary treatments is essential. Blood-based biomarkers provide a novel method for evaluating brain injury. The ability of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light chain (NfL), neuron-specific enolase (NSE) and total-tau (t-tau) to measure white and grey matter injury is unestablished in comatose OHCA survivors treated with targeted temperature management (TTM) or xenon combined with TTM. We examined correlations between the biomarkers and white and grey matter injury assessed with diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). This was a randomized, single-blind, phase 2 clinical drug trial involving two multipurpose intensive care units in Finland. It was conducted between August 2009 and March 2015. One hundred and ten comatose OHCA patients aged 24 to 76 years were randomly assigned to either inhaled xenon treatment combined with 24-h TTM (33°C) (n = 55, xenon group) or TTM alone (n = 55, control group). MRI data were available from 96 patients, with a median imaging time of 53 h (interquartile range, 47-64 h) after OHCA. Biomarker data were obtained from 105 patients. In the control group of 48 patients, after adjusting for age, sex and site, a disruption of white matter microintegrity as measured by decreased fractional anisotropy (FA) of DTI, the primary endpoint of the trial, showed a significant negative correlation with NfL at 24, 48 and 72 h (ρ = -0.28 to -0.37; P < 0.05), NSE at 48 and 72 h (ρ = -0.30 to -0.35; P < 0.05) and t-tau only at 72 h (ρ = -0.30; P < 0.05). In the xenon group (n = 48), these correlations were absent at all timepoints. The NfL-FA partial correlations showed progressive divergence between the xenon and control groups, with a statistically significant between-group difference observed at 72 h (ρ = -0.37 versus ρ = 0.14; P = 0.016). Cortical or basal ganglia grey matter mean diffusivity did not have a consistent correlation with biomarker levels at different time points. No statistically significant differences were found between the xenon and control groups in the adjusted geometric mean levels of GFAP, NfL, NSE or t-tau at various time points following OHCA. In conclusion, NfL correlated with FA in controls but not in the xenon group. This between-group difference reached significance at 72 h, suggesting that xenon may modify the relationship between axonal injury and white matter microstructure after OHCA.

title: Loss of microbial diversity from human-microbe coevolution: immune, epigenetic, and enteric nervous system mechanisms linking dysbiosis to neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Homo sapiens are the only species of humans still existing, as far as we know. Sapiens became the "sensible, shrewd, knowing" species of humanoids (the Homo genus) with assistance from the gut microbiota that evolved alongside and within Homo sapiens, providing metabolites and assisting the gut-brain axis to aid brain expansion and function. This review discusses coevolution, how dietary and environmental changes have influenced the importance of the gut microbiota, the microbiome-gut-brain axis (MGBA) and related epigenetic changes, and how current procedures and products may alter the beneficial commensal relationship and contribute to increased incidence of disorders such as asthma, autoimmune diseases, obesity, and neuropathology. Immune and endocrine homeostasis are tightly linked to the MGBA, and industrialization, by dispersing more chemicals into the environment, is upsetting the balance. Although brain laterization influences on immunity and neurological disorders are reported, there is no definitive linkage between brain hemisphere effects on gut microbiota or the MGBA. Brain laterality (left/right hemisphere differences) affects physical and mental stress sensitivity, but linkage of MGBA and metabolites to autoimmune neurological diseases remain speculative. Loss of microbiota diversity and altered proportions of certain bacterial species due to environmental stressors may lead to increased numbers of opportunistic and pathogenic bacteria (dysbiosis) creating metabolites having fewer beneficial and more detrimental effects across multiple host organs. Diet, environmental toxicants, and stress are presented as influences on the current increased incidence of some immune-associated disorders, autoimmune diseases, and neuropathy. Increased toxic insults are hypothesized to coincide with immune disorders based on gut microbiota changes. Within the CNS itself, complement- and immunoglobulin-mediated synaptic pruning has emerged as a convergent mechanism linking peripheral immune dysregulation to synaptic vulnerability in neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disease, suggesting that enteric nervous system and MGBA disruption may act upstream of these processes. Genetic and genomic aspects of the host-microbiome relationship are also discussed.

title: In situ delivery of cannabidiol-loaded GelMA sponge attenuates cerebral edema and neuroinflammation in traumatic brain injury.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a major cause of severe disability, and its secondary injury remains a key focus of interventional research. Cannabidiol (CBD) has neuroprotective potential, but conventional systemic administration still has limitations. In this study, we fabricated an in situ-implantable cannabidiol-loaded gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) sponge (GM-CBD) with short-term cytocompatibility and hemocompatibility and no detectable in vivo abnormalities. Under a non-equivalent dosing regimen, GM-CBD and intraperitoneally injected CBD (10 mg/kg) showed distinct concentration-distribution profiles: in the GM-CBD group, CBD continuously accumulated in the perilesional cortex over 48 h, whereas serum CBD remained persistently low. In a rat Feeney model of TBI, combined behavioral and neuropathological evaluation identified a single sponge loaded with a nominal 15 μg CBD as the working dose. At this dose, GM-CBD reduced neurological deficit scores, altered locomotor and exploratory behaviors in TBI rats, and attenuated neuronal injury and apoptosis. GM-CBD concurrently upregulated tight junction proteins and CD31+ endothelial cell expression, downregulated GFAP⁺ astrocyte proliferation, and altered AQP4 distribution, thereby improving blood-brain barrier integrity and alleviating post-traumatic cerebral edema. Furthermore, GM-CBD decreased IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α levels, increased IL-10, and inhibited microglial activation, suggesting attenuated acute neuroinflammation after TBI. Transcriptomic sequencing further showed that GM-CBD-associated differentially expressed genes were mainly involved in immune, stress, and inflammatory responses, with significant enrichment of the NF-κB, PI3K-Akt, and TNF signaling pathways. In summary, GM-CBD provides an in situ sustained-release strategy that exerts neuroprotection by attenuating post-traumatic cerebral edema and neuroinflammation.

title: Malignant cerebral edema secondary to herpes simplex virus encephalitis requiring decompressive hemicraniectomy.
abstract: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) is a severe viral infection of the central nervous system that most commonly affects the temporal lobes and limbic structures. Although most cases are managed medically with intravenous acyclovir, rare cases can rapidly progress to malignant cerebral edema, mass effect, and neurologic deterioration requiring surgical intervention. We report the case of a 57-year-old woman presenting with altered mental status, headache, vomiting, myalgias, and focal neurologic deficits. Initial computed tomography (CT) and CT angiography of the head and neck were unremarkable, but magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated diffusion restriction involving the right mesial temporal lobe and insular cortex.
