At least one dysmorphological abnormality was identified in 25/28 patients (89.3%), and multidistrict vascular involvement was observed in 20/29 individuals (69.0%) of our selected cohort of sCeAD patients. Vascular abnormalities beyond the cervicocephalic region were detected in 17 patients (58.6%). Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants considered clinically relevant to the vascular phenotype were identified in two patients of our selected cohort of sCeAD patients (6.9%). Our findings suggest that dysmorphological features and multidistrict vascular involvement may help identify sCeAD patients who are more likely to benefit from genetic testing.

title: Self-report measures of mindfulness for children: convergent validity, predictive validity, and impacts of social desirability bias.
abstract: Mindfulness-based interventions have shown promise in supporting psychological well-being in children. However, mindfulness is commonly measured using self-report questionnaires, a method that might be problematic due to its reliance on children's accurate self-perceptions of their own mindfulness and the potential influence of social desirability bias. In the current study, we examined the convergent validity, the predictive validity, and the influence of social desirability bias on three mindfulness self-report measures for children ages 9-13 years (N = 109). Results showed that children's self-reported mindfulness demonstrated good convergent validity and predictive validity, as higher levels of self-reported mindfulness were positively associated with higher levels of parent-reported executive functioning. Self-reported mindfulness also covaried with social desirability bias. However, controlling for this bias did not substantively affect the convergent validity nor the predictive validity of self-reported mindfulness. These findings suggest that children's self-reported mindfulness also captures social desirability bias, but this bias may not affect conclusions about mindfulness when assessed as a latent factor across multiple measures. Future work measuring children's mindfulness with self-reports should account for social desirability bias when possible, as well as explore objective methods of assessing mindfulness in children.

title: Comparison of visual tasks for assessing attentional bias in cannabis users and non-users.
abstract: Attentional bias toward substance-related cues is a key feature of addiction and may contribute to the continued use of substances, such as cannabis. However, the sensitivity of different paradigms for detecting this bias remains underexplored. This study compared three visual attentional bias paradigms: dot probe (DP), eye movement (EM), and MouseView.js (MV) in detecting cannabis-related attentional biases among cannabis users and non-users. Thirty-one participants (i.e., 16 users and 15 non-users) completed all measures: DP (reaction time to probes replacing cannabis or neutral stimuli), EM (measured via eye-tracking), and MV (cursor-based dwell time). Linear mixed-effects models examined the effects of stimulus type, group, craving, and cannabis use severity. The EM and MV tasks revealed significant stimulus effects, with non-users showing greater attention to neutral images, while cannabis users exhibited more evenly distributed attention across stimuli. In the EM task, a significant stimulus × severity interaction indicated reduced attentional differentiation with increased cannabis use severity. MV results followed a similar, but less precise pattern. In contrast, the DP task showed minimal group or interaction effects and lacked sensitivity to detect attentional differences. These findings suggest that EM-based measures are more sensitive for detecting cannabis-related attentional biases, particularly when accounting for cannabis use severity. MV showed some alignment with EM patterns but demonstrated weaker effects. The DP task, despite its widespread use, may be insufficient for capturing cannabis-related attentional differences. Results highlight the importance of task selection in attentional bias research and the potential influence of individual differences in cannabis use severity.

title: Safety and feasibility of accelerated deep transcranial magnetic stimulation for stimulant use disorder: A pilot study.
abstract: Stimulant use disorder (StUD) remains a major public health concern with limited treatment options and high attrition. Deep transcranial magnetic stimulation (dTMS) targeting the medial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices may modulate circuits involved in craving and control. This pilot study evaluated the safety, tolerability, and feasibility of accelerated dTMS (adTMS) using the H7 coil in individuals with moderate to severe StUD. In this open-label, single-arm feasibility trial, participants received 30 sessions of high-frequency (20 Hz) adTMS using the H7 coil (three daily sessions delivered over 10 days). Primary outcomes were feasibility and safety. Secondary outcomes included craving (SCQ-B; daily visual analog scale), and stimulant use (Timeline Follow-Back, urine toxicology). Exploratory outcomes, including changes in depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), withdrawal (SSSA), and rumination (RRS) were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models. 19 participants enrolled, 16 initiated treatment, and 12 (75% of those who initiated treatment) completed ≥80% of sessions. Among these 12 treatment completers, retention was 67% at 2 and 4 weeks and 58% at 12 weeks. No serious adverse events occurred; the most frequent side effects were mild headache (75%) and fatigue (69%). Depressive symptoms (p=.020) and withdrawal severity (p=.033) improved significantly, while changes in anxiety, rumination, craving, and stimulant use did not (p>.05). Our adTMS protocol was safe and well tolerated in individuals with StUD. Retention was similar to what has been observed in other trials in this population, but refining retention strategies may help decrease attrition. Depression and withdrawal scores decreased over time, but not craving or stimulant use. Larger, sham-controlled studies with optimized retention strategies are warranted to determine efficacy.

title: A unified general cognitive factor explains impairment across schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, OCD and substance use disorder.
abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that cognitive impairment cuts across traditional psychiatric diagnoses and may reflect a shared underlying cognitive liability. We examined whether a general cognitive factor (gFc) accounts for transdiagnostic deficits across schizophrenia (SZ), bipolar disorder (BD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and substance use disorder (SUD). A total of 797 individuals [544 affected and 253 healthy controls (HC)] completed a standardized cognitive battery. Bifactor confirmatory factor analysis was used to derive general cognitive factor (gFc) and domain-specific impairments (cognitive flexibility, working memory, new learning and social cognition). Model fit supported the bifactor structure. Linear mixed-effect models, with family as random effect, and demographic variables as fixed effect evaluated transdiagnostic and diagnosis specific impairments. The gFc was significantly reduced across all diagnoses groups relative to HC, [B(SE): BD -0.49 (0.07), OCD -0.21 (0.07), SUD -0.43(0.08), SZ -0.76 (0.08), all p < 0.001]; verbal learning showed additional diagnosis-specific deficits, most pronounced in SZ [B (SE):0.59 (0.09)] and BD[B(SE):0.48 (0.09)], both p < 0.001. A single gFc accounts for substantial cognitive dysfunction across major psychiatric disorders, while verbal-learning impairment appears diagnosis-specific. These findings support a dimensional architecture of cognition in psychiatry and identify gFc as a promising transdiagnostic target for clinical and mechanistic research.

title: Predicting individual differences in social functioning from functional connectomes in children with autism spectrum disorder.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by profound heterogeneity in social functioning. While previous studies using group-level comparisons and predefined regions of interest have identified neural correlates of social deficits in ASD, the neural basis of individual differences in social functioning remains unclear. Here, we applied connectome-based predictive modeling to resting-state functional MRI data from 65 children with ASD aged 1.5-8 years (mean age = 4.23 years) to predict individual differences in social functioning assessed by the personal-social subscale of the Griffiths Development Scales (GDS). Results showed that whole-brain functional connectivity significantly predicted personal-social scores. The positive predictive network was dominated by connections within the default mode network, with the left precuneus emerging as a core hub. In contrast, the negative predictive network mainly involved inter-network connections, particularly between the frontoparietal and sensorimotor networks. In an independent cohort of 27 children with ASD aged 1.25-8 years (mean age = 3.31 years), the positive-edge model showed a significant association with personal-social scores, whereas the negative-edge and combined models did not. These findings suggest that intrinsic large-scale brain network organization is associated with individual differences in social functioning in children with ASD, highlighting the potential of network-level approaches for characterizing neurodevelopmental heterogeneity and supporting future precision-oriented research.

title: Childhood sexual abuse, marital discord, and marital disruption: Propensity score analyses.
abstract: Childhood sexual abuse (CSA) is associated with greater relationship discord and a higher likelihood of marital disruption; however, these associations may be confounded by co-occurring childhood adversities and sociodemographic factors. Propensity score methods, which seek to improve comparability between exposed and unexposed groups on observed characteristics, provide a complementary approach to traditional covariate adjustment for addressing measured confounding. To examine the association between CSA and marital discord and disruption using traditional covariate and propensity score methods. Participants were from the National Comorbidity Survey Replication, a nationally representative probability sample of United States adults. Associations between CSA and marital discord and disruption were examined using four approaches: bivariate (unadjusted), traditional covariate-adjusted, propensity score-adjusted, and propensity score matching (PSM) analyses. Covariates included demographic and childhood characteristics. Post-matching models additionally adjusted for covariates with residual absolute standardized differences ≥0.10. CSA was associated with greater marital discord in the bivariate, traditional covariate-adjusted, propensity score-adjusted, and PSM analyses. After additional post-matching covariate adjustment, the estimated association remained positive and similar in magnitude. CSA was associated with higher odds of marital disruption across all models, including the post-matching covariate-adjusted model. For both marital outcomes, estimates were consistent in direction and similar in magnitude across traditional covariate-adjusted and propensity score approaches, which address measured confounding differently. Future research should investigate underlying mechanisms using longitudinal and dyadic designs.

title: Complement C3a plays a role in diabetic cardiomyopathy mainly via C3aR-ERK-PANoptosis pathway.
abstract: Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is one of the leading causes of death in diabetic patients. However, the pathogenesis of DCM remains incompletely understood, and effective targeted therapies are lacking. This study aims to investigate the role of complement C3a in the development of DCM, providing a novel theoretical foundation for its precise prevention and treatment. Eight-week-old male C57BL/6 J mice were injected with streptozotocin (STZ) to induce a diabetes model for 26 weeks. The two intervention groups were injected with C3a receptor antagonist (SB290157, 30 mg/kg/d) and novel C3 cleavage inhibitor (CP40-KK, 2 mg/kg/d) by intraperitoneal injection for 8 weeks. Cardiac function/histopathological changes were determined by echocardiogram examination, and Millar catheter system. Human cardiomyocytes (AC16) were employed in vitro. C3a was significantly upregulated in the plasma of the STZ-induced DCM model, and PANoptosis plays a critical role in cardiac tissue and cardiomyocytes. The C3a receptor antagonist (SB290157) could significantly improve the cardiac function of diabetic mice, reduce myocardial hypertrophy, and inhibit the activation level of PANoptosis pathway in cardiac tissue. Furthermore, inhibiting the C3aR/ERK pathway could regulate cardiomyocyte PANoptosis by pyroptosis (NLRP3-dependent), apoptosis (caspase-3-dependent), and necroptosis (RIP-dependent) in the DCM model and C3a-treated cardiomyocytes. The novel complement C3 inhibitor CP40-KK exerts comparable therapeutic efficacy to SB290157 in treating DCM at a lower drug dosage. We demonstrate the crucial role of the C3a/C3aR signaling axis, and CP40-KK treatment was protective in the STZ-induced DCM model. These findings provide valuable evidence supporting potential complement-based therapies targeting the C3a/C3aR/ERK/PANoptosis pathway in DCM treatment.

title: No effect of transcranial direct current stimulation on brain age during cognitive behavioral therapy for major depressive disorder: secondary results from a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial.
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) has previously been associated with accelerated brain ageing, a feature reported to remain unchanged after antidepressant pharmacotherapy. We conducted a secondary analysis of a randomized trial augmenting cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), a long-established first-line treatment for depression, with active or sham transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), a newer neuromodulatory approach that has received FDA approval for MDD in at-home device format. We calculated the brain-predicted age difference (brain-PAD = predicted brain age - chronological age) in 38 unmedicated patients with MDD before and after treatment, using a model trained on anatomical MRI scans from N = 3377 healthy controls. Linear mixed-effects models tested change in brain-PAD and predicted brain age, adjusting for age and sex. The randomized comparison showed no evidence that active tDCS produced differential change in brain-PAD relative to sham (β = 0.85 years, 95% CI [-0.83, 2.53], p = .308, BF10 = 0.22). Contrary to our hypothesis, in the combined treated cohort (CBT ± tDCS), average change in brain-PAD was negligible (β = 0.01 years, 95% CI [-0.82, 0.84], p = .985, BF10 = 0.13), despite symptomatic improvement on the HAM-D. Baseline brain-PAD also did not differ among MDD patients, healthy controls, and first-degree relatives after adjustment for age and sex (F(2,93) = 1.31, p = .276, BF10 = 0.04). These findings suggest that short-term depression improvement and adjunctive tDCS were not accompanied by detectable changes in MRI-derived brain age or brain-PAD. However, our relatively young patients, small sample size, wide confidence intervals, limited local calibration, and unmeasured candidate moderators of the brain age constrain definitive conclusions. Larger, longer, and biologically stratified trials are needed to determine whether brain age biomarkers are modifiable and useful tools in clinical practice.

title: Unraveling the diagnostic dilemma in cerebral amyloid angiopathy: epileptic seizures or transient focal neurological episodes?
Distinct daytime sleepiness phenotypes across insomnia symptom dimensions in the Wisconsin sleep cohort.
abstract: Insomnia symptoms are heterogeneous, and it remains unclear whether difficulty initiating sleep (DIS), difficulty maintaining sleep (DMS), operationalized as repeated nighttime awakening, and early morning awakening (EMA) correspond to distinct joint patterns of subjective daytime sleepiness and physiological sleep propensity. We examined these symptom-specific phenotypes and their clinical burden. We analyzed 881 Wisconsin Sleep Cohort participants with complete Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) and Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) data. Four phenotypes were defined by ESS >10 and MSLT <8 min: Neither, Subjective-only, Objective-only, and Both. DIS, DMS, and EMA were assessed using self-reported questionnaire items and were entered simultaneously in adjusted multinomial logistic regression. Greater DIS severity was associated with lower ESS (β = -0.70, 95% confidence interval (CI) -1.02 to -0.39), longer MSLT latency (β = 0.45 min, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.80), and lower relative risk of Both (relative risk ratio (RRR) = 0.67, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.87). Greater DMS severity was associated with higher ESS (β = 0.43, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.66) and higher relative risk of Both (RRR = 1.30, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.56). EMA was not associated with the overall phenotype distribution. Within frequent DMS, Subjective-only sleepiness was associated with higher depression and trait anxiety after false discovery rate adjustment. DIS and DMS were associated with different daytime sleepiness profiles. Within frequent DMS, subjective sleepiness identified greater psychological burden. The observed associations were generally modest and support considering nocturnal symptom pattern when interpreting daytime sleepiness.

title: The role of nanomedicine in infectious diseases of the central nervous system: a narrative review.
abstract: Infectious diseases in the central nervous system (CNS) are a global health problem, causing significant morbidity and mortality. One of the main challenges in treating CNS infections is the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which limits drug delivery to the brain. During infections, brain-resident immune cells, release inflammatory mediators, which further contribute to neuroinflammation and damage. Nanomedicine offers an alternative for CNS treatment that has been explored in several types of infections. Across preclinical studies, nanomedicine approaches have demonstrated substantial improvements in CNS delivery and therapeutic outcomes, including reductions in brain pathogen burden of up to 3 log10 colony-forming units, increases in brain drug concentrations of 3-4-fold, and survival improvements of up to 100% in selected infection models. However, the literature remains fragmented across pathogens, nanomaterial platforms, and experimental models, with few direct comparisons and limited clinical validation. This review provides a comprehensive, up-to-date synthesis of the current evidence, integrating emerging nanomedicine strategies across major CNS infections while highlighting common therapeutic approaches, clinical applications, limitations, and key gaps that must be addressed to advance these technologies toward clinical translation. It also highlights advances and techniques in nanomedicine for treating brain infections, discusses clinical applications, and promotes innovation and future directions.

title: Adverse Childhood Experiences, Emotional-Cognitive Profiles, and Response to Cognitive Remediation and Emotion Skills Training in Anorexia Nervosa.
journal: European eating disorders review : the journal of the Eating Disorders Association
abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) involves restrictive eating and marked difficulties in emotion regulation and cognitive flexibility. Cognitive Remediation and Emotion Skills Training (CREST) targets these domains, but outcomes may vary by psychological profile and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). This study examined the associations of emotional-cognitive profiles and ACEs with treatment response following CREST in inpatients with AN. We studied 198 female inpatients with AN who completed baseline and post-treatment assessments after an 8-week group CREST programme. Cluster analysis of the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), Toronto Alexithymia Scale-20 (TAS-20), Detail and Flexibility Questionnaire (DFLEX), and Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R) identified subgroups. Outcomes (ΔEDE-Q, ΔDFLEX, ΔTAS, ΔBMI) were compared across clusters. Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) subscales were tested in multinomial regression and moderation models. Three clusters emerged: Cluster 1 (low impairment), Cluster 0 (moderate impairment), and Cluster 2 (globally impaired). Groups differed in age, illness duration, BMI, and adversities exposure (all p < 0.05). Psychological outcomes differed: ΔDFLEX (H = 63.7, p < 0.001) and ΔTAS (p < 0.001), with Cluster 2 showing the greatest gains. Emotional abuse was positively associated with both the moderate and globally impaired profiles, whereas physical abuse specifically predicted the globally impaired profile. Sexual abuse was inversely associated with both impaired profiles. Moderation analyses indicated that associations between ACE severity and psychological change varied across emotional-cognitive profiles, with direction and magnitude differing by outcome and ACE subtype. Greater short-term psychological changes were observed in the globally impaired profile, although baseline severity warrants cautious interpretation. Adverse childhood experiences were associated with profile membership and heterogeneous patterns of psychological change across profiles.

title: Protocol for integrated phosphoproteomic and proteomic analysis of the mouse ventral tegmental area with functional and kinase motif enrichment.
abstract: We present a protocol for label-free proteomic and phosphoproteomic analysis of the mouse ventral tegmental area (VTA). We describe steps for combining region-specific biopsy-punch collection, parallel proteomic and phosphoproteomic processing, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), and downstream enrichment analysis. We detail procedures for SynGO-based synaptic localization, g:Profiler/DAVID pathway enrichment, and iceLogo/pLogo motif analysis. This protocol enables quantitative assessment of protein abundance, phosphorylation dynamics, and functional interpretation from limited brain region samples. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Diezel et al.1.

title: Extracellular vesicles and immune-glial remodeling in lung cancer brain metastasis: potential intersections with exercise-related myokines.
abstract: Lung cancer brain metastasis develops through reciprocal interactions between metastatic tumor cells and a brain-specific vascular, glial, and immune microenvironment. Tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) can participate in this process by altering blood-brain barrier (BBB) properties, influencing brain-directed distribution, and transferring regulatory cargo to endothelial and myeloid recipient cells. This review integrates direct evidence from non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) brain or central nervous system metastasis with related lung cancer EV studies, while distinguishing these findings from cross-cancer mechanistic evidence. We first describe the transition from the BBB to the heterogeneous blood-tumor barrier and distinguish the contributions of astrocytes, resident microglia, recruited monocyte-derived macrophages, and T cells. We then examine how defined EV cargo, including lnc-MMP2-2, LINC00482, miR-21, L1CAM, and miR-374a-5p, affects barrier integrity, myeloid state, or brain-metastatic behavior. Myeloid responses are interpreted according to cellular origin and function rather than by a fixed M1/M2 binary. Exercise-related myokines and exerkines are considered separately as a hypothesis-generating systemic layer that could influence tumor-cell EV production, deliver signals through muscle-derived EVs, or alter recipient-cell responsiveness; none of these routes has yet been established as a causal mechanism in lung cancer brain metastasis. Together, current evidence supports a role for EV-mediated vascular and immune/glial communication in lung cancer brain metastasis, while leaving the contribution of exercise-related signals unresolved.

title: Network-guided Thalamic Neuromodulation for Epilepsy.
abstract: This review takes a network-based perspective on thalamic neuromodulation for epilepsy, examining how each target (e.g., anterior (ANT), centromedian (CM), and pulvinar (PUL) thalamic nuclei) engage distinct seizure networks, what evidence supports each, and how stimulation/electrophysiologic mapping can guide individualized targeting rather than a fixed, syndrome-based approach. Randomized and prospective trials have expanded the evidence for ANT and CM stimulation, while emerging data support the pulvinar as a target for posterior quadrant and temporal lobe epilepsies. Syndrome-specific sweet-spot analyses reveal distinct optimal sites within the CM for LGS and IGE. Thalamic sEEG with single-pulse stimulation and trials of DBS-style stimulation now enables characterization of seizure network engagement and identification of acute biomarkers that may inform target and parameter selection. Multi-target strategies combining thalamic nuclei, or thalamic and cortical leads, show preliminary promise for broadly distributed seizure networks. No single thalamic target is uniformly effective across epilepsy types; optimal targeting requires individualized, network-informed characterization. This supports a shift toward connectomic and individualized approaches, with future work needed to refine target selection, stimulation paradigms, and individualized optimization using clinical outcomes and electrophysiological biomarkers.
